endorsements.quote: ID communities should establish structured educational programs to help clinicians develop a working knowledge of AI, its applications, and its limitations.
AI augmented workflow may use AI to assist in summarizing data, highlighting risks, and making preliminary assessments, but final decision-making would remain clinician driven.
Simple, well-defined tasks—such as flagging inappropriate antibiotic prescriptions or detecting missing infection control documentations—may be safely handled by AI as first use cases.

unlisted_practices: ID clinicians should collaborate with data scientists and clinical informaticists to standardize ID-related definitions, antimicrobial use metrics, and acceptable diagnostic criteria when automation is deemed appropriate.

ID communities should establish AI interest groups and committees and create partnerships with AI developers to ensure AI tools are clinically validated, ethically designed, and aligned with real-world ID challenges.
ID professional societies should issue position statements, regulatory guidance, and best practices for AI oversight in ID care and operations.
Clinicians should advocate for higher quality, ID-specific data pipelines to support AI.
Health systems should design equity checks across all AI lifecycle stages for AI solutions integrated in ID practice.
Health systems should support protected time and continuing education for AI learning and integrate AI literacy into training curricula.

screen.reason: This is a commentary/perspective discussing AI literacy, governance, and the integration of agentic AI into infectious disease clinical practice.
